verification.note: Confirmed, and it is a coverage gap rather than an application defect. The harness deliberately does not mint CUSIPs -- its docstring argues, correctly, that inventing security identifiers inside a provenance-first ledger is worse than omitting them. The consequence is that no persona run can ever exercise the ownership bridge, which is the tab's headline capability. That the feature works was established outside the harness, against the real ledger, where GOOG and GOOGL resolve to distinct tickers off distinct CUSIPs. Recorded so a future run does not re-file it as a defect.

why_it_matters: This is a testing-process finding, not an application defect -- the bridge's logic (read directly: catalog.py's ledger_cusip_tickers and apply_tickers) looks correct and deliberately conservative (no name-based fallback matching). But every persona run against this harness will report the same 'no badges anywhere' observation for a structural reason that has nothing to do with whether the feature works, and a maintainer triaging feedback.jsonl across runs with no verification pass could easily misread that as five separate confirmations of a broken bridge. Worth a harness fixture (e.g. one synthetic CUSIP-bearing broker row per session, or a documented seed script) so a future run can actually exercise the ownership badge rather than only reading the code that would produce it.

title: Institutions page never tells the reader that an unbadged row can still be something they own

verification.note: Confirmed, filed independently by two runs on the same day, and the evidence is stronger than either reported. The badge requires a CUSIP match, and only the Robinhood adapter supplies CUSIPs at all: `sofi.py` and `webull.py` both hard-code `cusip=None` because neither export has the column. Counted against the real ledger: 119 of 218 instruments carry a CUSIP, so 45% can never be flagged. The concrete case is the worst one available. Apple is the largest position in Berkshire's disclosed book at 22.03% of it; the user holds AAPL; AAPL is one of the instruments with no CUSIP, so it renders unflagged. The 'only holdings I also own' filter therefore hid a position the user does own, while implying the hidden set was not owned. Fixed with a caveat beside both filters stating that an unflagged row means no CUSIP match rather than no ownership.

why_it_matters: This is exactly the persona's own stated reflex (see uat/personas/pro-investor-01.md: 'Partial data is labelled, not hidden'). A reader deciding whether an institution's trim in a name they hold is worth a second look has no signal that the absence of a badge is uninformative rather than a negative result -- the page's only self-description of what the badge means is written for the case where it appears, never for the much more common case where it doesn't.

title: Unidentified $12M position renders as literal 'N/A'/'LEI:N/A' text, indistinguishable from an error

verification.note: Confirmed, and worse than reported. `_resolve_nport_key` tested the `N/A` sentinel on the CUSIP only; the ISIN and LEI branches checked emptiness alone. Reproduced against the live filing: QQQ's CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 future has `<name>`, `<lei>` and `<cusip>` all equal to the literal string `N/A`, so it keyed on `LEI:N/A`, displayed an issuer called `N/A`, and carried -$12,012,436.80 badged NEW in the same styling as an equity purchase. ARK's OpenAI position hit the same branch at $177,028,452.35. The display was the lesser problem: `LEI:N/A` is a key two rows can share, so two unidentifiable rows in one filing would be grouped and summed into a single position that no filing reported. The rows are not actually anonymous -- that future carries `<title>CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 Index Future</title>` and `<ticker value="NQM6"/>`, both of which the resolver was ignoring. Fixed: the sentinel is tested at every step, `<ticker>` joins the chain ahead of the LEI (an LEI names the counterparty, not the instrument), `<title>` supplies the issuer name when `<name>` is a sentinel, and a per-row ordinal is the terminal fallback so the key cannot collide by construction. Verified live: the row now reads `TICKER:NQM6` / `CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 Index Future`, and every key in the filing is unique.

why_it_matters: This is the provenance test the persona applies literally: 'a number whose derivation I cannot reconstruct is a number I will not act on.' A -$12M swing with no identity and an apparent negative weight is very plausibly a legitimate derivative or short-notional line NPORT-P allows funds to report (the page does cover 'everything the fund owns', not equities alone) -- but nothing on the page says so, and as rendered it is genuinely unclear whether this is real fund data or a parse failure.

verification.note: The observation is accurate -- the tab sits outside the persona's five-step decision loop and is labelled as research. why_it_matters: This bounds how the feature should be marketed/positioned: for a swing trader on a one-to-several-week horizon (this persona's actual mandate), the Institutions tab is correctly scoped as diligence/context, not a signal source, and the page's own copy already sets that expectation correctly. A longer-horizon persona (multi-quarter allocator) is the profile for whom this page's cadence would actually match the decision cadence -- worth confirming with that persona rather than this one in a future run.
